I really enjoyed catching some of your streams over the last few months. I appreciate the attitude of "wonder" and "let's see what we can do" with these tools. I respect the honesty of admitting not knowing how to code, and it was genuinely cool to see how that is no longer a barrier to building tech. I also respect that you started learning.

With that said, I have watched as you've figured out the game of social media - drama, click baiting, etc. This, I was sorry to see, but I stuck around.

Many people have a lot to say about Theo. He has strong opinions, not always correct (as with any of us), but the one thing that is clear to anyone who has been in this space is that he does understand the difficult pieces of software devekopment and much of the CS field overall. This understanding is at a level very few ever get to.

When he offered to have an independent auditor check both, you met it with "he's just jealous."

Building cool stuff with vibe coding is great, but this is like asserting you can build a better pharmaceutical with a few prompts and no real knowledge of the field than someone with the background, who also uses the same tools.

Some humble advice, for what it is worth: I'd love to see you return to the honesty about what you don't know and take challenges with grace and as an opportunity to learn more and get better at what you do.

Attention gained by cheap tricks like drama and clickbait _feel_ free, but they aren't. They chip away at your reputation, and that is something that is very hard to ever regain. Once it's gone, it often stays gone. When all is said and done, you've traded your birthright for a bowl of beans.

This is said with a genuine hope for a bright future for you. You have a lot of road ahead, and you're sharp enough to do some very cool things. Hopefully you won't let the easy roads distract you from what you could do.

text:
Three rural Irish comedies by John McDwyer offer audiences an evening of sharp dialogue, unexpected twists, and characters who feel recognisably local rather than stage Irish. 

The Pension Plan centres on the bachelor Flanagan brothers, content on their hillside farm until a persistent neighbour and a visiting stranger threaten their settled life; expect madcap plotting and a guaranteed night of laughter that still leaves room for the price of easy solutions. 

Unforgiven, first staged in 2006, follows brothers waiting on their father’s death for very different reasons while a neighbour remains unaware of the plans being made for her; a returning brother from America sets the cats among the pigeons in a rapid succession of surprises and one-liners drawn from ordinary rural life. 

Turning Mammy, described by the author as a comedy with a few serious bits, tracks two sisters and their bachelor neighbour: one searching for a child given up at birth, the other waiting for a bed-bound mother to die so a long courtship can begin. Secrets surface, motives prove less simple than they appear, and the humour sits alongside genuine melancholy.

John McDwyer was born in Sooey, County Sligo, in 1947 and has lived most of his adult life in County Leitrim. After thirty-two years with AIB he co-founded Beezneez Theatre Company in 1997 and served as its artistic director through roughly forty tours until he stepped back from the road in 2024. 

His first radio play won an RTÉ award in 1992; later stage works, including the Leitrim Trilogy, have been taken up by amateur companies across Ireland and further afield. 

Directors and actors have noted the depth he gives ordinary people without reducing them to caricature. His plays continue to be licensed for performance, with recent outings of The Pension Plan at venues such as Hawk’s Well Theatre in Sligo and regional houses on the amateur circuit. He lists The Showgrounds among his favourite places.

In all of this, President Donald John Trump has violated the Article II, Section 1, Clause 8-mandated presidential oath of office to faithfully execute the office of President of the United States, and to the best of his ability, preserve, protect, and defend the Constitution of the United States; has abused the powers of the presidency by committing high crimes and misdemeanors, in a manner contrary to his trust as President; has detrimentally flouted the United States Constitution by operating vicious, quota-driven, unaccountable paramilitary forces 75 killing people (including Renée Good, Alex Pretti, Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, and Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero); and is now even closer to brazenly and wantonly devolving the United States democratic republic into an authoritarian regime, where, if left in office, unjustified killings of people and coverups by ICE and CBP are normalized to the great prejudice of the cause of law and justice, and to the manifest injury of the people of the United States.

Wherefore, Donald John Trump, by such conduct, warrants impeachment and trial, and removal from office.”

DEMOCRATS NEED STRATEGY FOR STRUGGLE, NOT PARLIAMENTARY CRETINISM

On Thursday, December 11, 2025, House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries, Democratic Whip Katherine Clark and Democratic Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar issued the following statement:
“Impeachment is a sacred constitutional vehicle designed to hold a corrupt executive accountable for abuse of power, breaking the law and violating the public trust. The effort traditionally requires a comprehensive investigative process, the collection and review of thousands of documents, an exacting scrutiny of the facts, the examination of dozens of key witnesses, Congressional hearings, sustained public organizing and the marshaling of the forces of democracy to build a broad national consensus. None of that serious work has been done, with the Republican majority focused solely on rubber stamping Donald Trump’s extreme agenda. Accordingly, we will be voting “present” on today’s motion to table the impeachment resolution as we continue our fight to make life more affordable for everyday Americans.”

This approach to the vital impeachment question might have been adequate for times of greater tranquility than our own, but this overly cautious, slow, and fundamentally timid strategy is wholly inadequate for the present acute crisis, when decisive action is required. Most obviously, the House leadership appears oblivious to the grievous damage being done by Trump and his gang to the United States and the free world, day by day, hour by hour. American citizens have been wantonly gunned down by ICE raids which have not stopped. The illegal abolition of USAID humanitarian assistance has already caused hundreds of thousands of deaths in less-developed countries, particularly in Africa, and this death toll is likely to rise into the millions unless USAID is quickly restored for the purposes directed by Congress. The pursuit of an early victory in the Iran war is being prevented by Trump’s ineffective, weak, and vacillating misleadership. Ukrainians are needlessly dying because of Trump’s vindictive refusal to provide necessary weaponry which the United States could supply without damaging our homeland defense. Most of all, one shudders to think of the dangerous and unstable combination of defeatist appeasement and enraged flight forward adventurism that might characterize Trump’s behavior in an actual strategic crisis of the type Putin and Xi are capable of triggering at any moment. Under these circumstances, it is simply not realistic to carry out the lengthy and time-consuming set piece preparations envisioned by the House Democratic leaders. They must urgently develop an emergency plan for impeachment. If Democratic Party gains in the upcoming midterms are as large as the polls suggest they will be, the need for laborious preparations to help create a consensus for impeachment will become largely irrelevant.

REP. MASSIE (R-KY): IMPEACH HEGSETH RESOLUTION

What follows is a condensed version of Congressmen Massie’s resolution; as always, the full texts of impeachment resolutions should be available on the website of the relevant House sponsor.

Impeaching Peter Brian Hegseth, Secretary of Defense, for high crimes and misdemeanors.

Resolved, That Peter Brian Hegseth, Secretary of Defense, also referred to as Secretary of War by the Administration, is impeached for high crimes and misdemeanors and that the following articles of impeachment be exhibited to the United States Senate: Articles of impeachment exhibited by the House of Representatives of the United States of America in the name of itself and of the people of the United States of America, against Peter Brian Hegseth, Secretary of Defense, in maintenance and support of its impeachment against him for high crimes and misdemeanors.

in ARTICLE II: WAGING WAR IN CONTRAVENTION OF THE WAR POWERS RESOLUTION OF 1973 SECTION 5(c)
ARTICLE III: WAGING WAR IN CONTRAVENTION OF THE WAR POWERS RESOLUTION OF 1973 SECTION 5(b)

ARTICLE V: EXTRAJUDICIAL KILLINGS
ARTICLE VI: SUPPRESSING FREE SPEECH
ARTICLE VII: KIDNAPPING OF A SOVERIGN FOREIGN LEADER
ARTICLE VIII: UNLAWFUL WAR IN YEMEN

Congressmen Massie’s bill of impeachment against Hegseth is useful first of all because it shows the breadth of hostility to MAGA misrule, even among Republicans. Secondly, it provides another useful warning that all articles of impeachment are not equal. Some have merit, and some do not. Some are even dangerous. Since articles of impeachment are voted on individually, and one at a time, it is important to distinguish between articles with meritorious policy consequences on the one hand, and weak or confused articles which lead in the wrong direction, on the other. With these latter, successful passage may create very dangerous legal precedents or present an image of weakness to aggressive foreign enemies like the CRINKs. But fortunately, the passage of a single article of impeachment is all it takes to put a lawless President, cabinet officer, or any other federal official on trial in the Senate. One article is all it takes!

In Massie’s bill of impeachment, Article VI in defense of free speech is clearly meritorious and should be passed, thus putting the wrecker Hegseth into the Senate dock.  This is obviously the article which should be approved.  The articles that rely on the Vietnam era War Powers Act are by contrast very weak because of the dubious constitutionality of this law, which has never survived review in the Supreme Court. The War Powers Act can be seen as attempting to wrongly resolve an ambiguity which the framers of the Constitution showed they expressly wanted kept open by making the president the commander-in-chief of the military forces, while at the same time specifying that only Congress can declare war. The question of which should prevail in any given situation is left open. Sometimes the silences of the Constitution can have an exceptional importance. The same considerations apply to the issue of whether a war in Yemen is legal or not. Laws aimed at reducing civilian casualties are probably unenforceable, and violate the time-tested wisdom that a war cannot be run by a committee, much less by an entire house of Congress. Extrajudicial killings of alleged drug dealers are likely in the same category. Foreign sovereign leaders can have no automatic immunity for acts committed against the United States. In short, Congressmen Massie’s articles reflect to a considerable degree a Republican or libertarian-isolationist and antigovernment mentality.  He should have referred an article of impeachment identifying Hegseth as trampling on the Constitution by failing to provide for the common defense -- as government is commanded to do in the Preamble -- by his firing on various transparent pretexts of some twenty-seven flag officers regarded as potentially anti-Trump, thus doing grievous long-term damage to the US officer corps.

OUR VOTE IS WORTH MORE THAN $5,000

GACETA MIGRANTE / Tonatiuh Cuazitl

Donald Trump has just put a number on the electoral table: $5,000.

The condition is political: a Republican victory in the House of Representatives and the Senate.

The election is close. Just a handful of districts could determine who controls the House.

This is where we come in.

The United States is approaching the midterm elections with tens of millions of Hispanic citizens eligible to vote. But one state deserves particular attention:

Texas.

Pew Research Center estimates that 6.7 million Hispanics are eligible to vote in Texas.

That is roughly 32 out of every 100 eligible voters in the state. Texas has the second-largest Hispanic electorate in the United States, behind only California.

And in Texas, the word Hispanic carries a particular historical weight.

Mexicans have long constituted, by far, the largest component of the state’s Latino electorate. In Pew’s detailed analysis of the Hispanic electorate in Texas, 87% were of Mexican origin. We are not applying that older percentage to today’s electorate to manufacture a current Mexican-American figure. It does, however, tell us which community has historically formed the backbone of Latino political power in Texas.

Now look at the 2026 electoral map.

UnidosUS identifies five Texas congressional districts among its battlegrounds with a significant Latino presence:

TX-15, TX-23, TX-28, TX-34 and TX-35.

Four of the districts in its current database alone account for more than 1.19 million registered Latino voters:

TX-15: 308,803
TX-28: 354,623
TX-34: 305,766
TX-35: 229,175

Look at TX-34.

305,766 registered Latino voters.

The Republican margin cited by UnidosUS for that contest is just 20,435 votes.

The registered Latino electorate is almost 15 times that margin.

That does not mean 305,766 people will vote for the same party.

They won’t.

It means a fraction of that electorate has enough political weight to alter the outcome of a competitive election.

The polling is also showing movement.

In May, UnidosUS surveyed 500 registered Latino voters in Texas, including a specific sample from battleground congressional districts.

77% said they were certain or almost certain to vote in November.

Among those who voted for Donald Trump in 2024, 20% said they would no longer vote for him today.

Texas.
Houston.
Ronaldo Salgado’s vote counts.

His father, Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, a 52-year-old Mexican man, left for work on July 7.

He never came home.

An ICE agent shot him during an immigration enforcement operation.

That gives the $5,000 a different meaning.

Washington can offer a dividend.

In Texas, a community of 6.7 million eligible Hispanic voters can put its own questions on the table.

Who answers for Lorenzo?

Who holds ICE accountable?

Who will require agents to be identifiable, body cameras to be used, use-of-force protocols to be public, and independent investigations when someone dies during a federal operation?

Who is willing to take those demands to Congress?

This is not about telling a Mexican American to vote Republican.

Nor Democrat.

It is about understanding the value of our vote before giving it away.

When a community represents nearly one-third of the Texas electorate, when hundreds of thousands of its voters are concentrated in contested districts, and when control of the House can depend on only a handful of seats, that community ceases to be a statistic.

It becomes political power.

Trump has put his number on the table:

$5,000.

Texas has another:

6.7 million.

And Lorenzo Salgado Araujo leaves us with the question no dividend can buy:

What is it worth to have our fathers come home alive?

Lorenzo can no longer vote.

Ronaldo can.

And so can millions like him.

OUR VOTE IS WORTH MORE THAN $5,000

We are not an audience — we are a community.

She told Global News in November 2023 that a B.C. surgeon said she was inoperable, that chemotherapy would buy little time, and that she was offered MAID — twice, by her account. She found surgeons who do debulking surgery plus heated intraperitoneal chemotherapy (HIPEC). In early 2023 she was treated by Dr. Armando Sardi at Mercy Medical Center in Baltimore, at a reported cost of more than $200,000, partly raised online.
